name: Indraneelaparuppatham (Neelachalanathar)
deity: Shiva as Neelachalanathar, Lord of the blue mountain, with the Goddess Neelambigai
period: A Himalayan Paadal Petra Sthalam of Vada Nadu, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century); its site is identified by tradition
dynasty: A sacred Himalayan mountain; no Tevaram-age temple is recorded
summary: Indraneelaparuppatham, the blue mountain that Indra worships, is a Himalayan shrine of the Tevaram that Sambandar sang from afar; tradition places it among the peaks around Badrinath.

sections.history: Indraneelaparuppatham — the mountain of the blue sapphire — is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the five in Vada Nadu, the northern country of the Tevaram. Thirugnana Sambandar sang a single pathigam to its Lord, praising the blue mountain to which Indra joins his hands in worship; tradition holds that he sang it, like other northern shrines, from Srikalahasti, never travelling to the Himalaya himself. Because the hymn names a mountain rather than a town, its place has been identified in more than one way: the tradition followed here sets it among the peaks around Badrinath, where the snow summit of Neelkanth rises, while other lists place it near Kathmandu in Nepal.
sections.architecture: No ancient temple of the Tevaram age is recorded for Indraneelaparuppatham; the sthalam is the mountain itself, and the name explains its form — clouds resting on its slopes are said to turn it blue. Tradition names its sacred water Indra Theertham. Pilgrims who honour it in the Badrinath valley do so before the great peaks above the Alaknanda, with Neelkanth, about 6,600 metres high, standing over the shrine town.
sections.legends: The sthala tradition gathers three stories here. Indra, king of the gods, is said to have worshipped Shiva on this mountain, giving it its name. Arjuna performed his penance here and received the Pashupata weapon from the Lord, who came to him as a hunter; and the demon Mukasura, who came in the form of a boar in that same episode, met his end at this place.
sections.festivals: There is no temple calendar of its own: the Tevaram shrine is honoured in the hymns, recited in Shaiva temples across the Tamil country, and by pilgrims during the summer season when the Badrinath valley is open. Maha Shivaratri and the Sambandar guru puja are times to recall it; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: For a Tamil Shaiva pilgrim, Indraneelaparuppatham is a shrine reached as much by the hymn as by the road: one looks up at the blue-white peaks above Badrinath and recites Sambandar's verses to the mountain Indra worships. It is a place to remember that the Tevaram's sacred map reaches from the Kaveri delta to the high Himalaya.

visit.timings: There are no temple timings for the mountain itself. The Badrinath valley is open to pilgrims only in the summer season, roughly from late April or May to November; confirm the current season locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Warm, layered clothing and sturdy footwear are needed at this altitude. Dress modestly at the shrines of Badrinath, and leave footwear outside temple premises.
visit.photography: The mountains and landscape may generally be photographed; follow the rules posted at the Badrinath temple and other shrines, where photography inside is restricted.
visit.gettingThere: Badrinath is reached by road from Rishikesh and Haridwar along the Alaknanda valley, via Joshimath. Rishikesh and Haridwar are the nearest major railheads, and Dehradun's Jolly Grant airport is the nearest airport. Roads in the hills can close in bad weather.
